scenes.heading: CRISPR and biochemical pathways
scenes.sub: Editing genes for more food and cleaner fuel
scenes.say: The world needs more food from the same farmland, and cleaner fuels. Both come back to biochemical pathways. CRISPR gives scientists a precise way to edit the genes for the enzymes in those pathways.

scenes.heading: CRISPR-Cas9 review
points: Guide RNA finds the target, next to a PAM
Repair with a template: insert or replace
scenes.say: Remember: find, cut, fix. The guide RNA finds the target sequence next to a PAM. Cas9 cuts both strands. A sloppy repair, called non-homologous end joining, usually knocks the gene out. Supply a template, and homology-directed repair can insert or replace a sequence.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A delivery can go to a house with a very similar address
scenes.science: Cas9 can cut DNA that closely matches the target: off-target effects
scenes.breaks: a driver makes one trip, but a cell has many Cas9–gRNA complexes, and the risk depends on how closely sequences match.
scenes.say: The guide RNA is like a delivery address. If another street has a very similar address, the order can go to the wrong door. Cas9 can cut DNA that closely matches the target too. That's an off-target effect, which is why edited plants are sequenced and screened.

scenes.heading: Better photosynthesis
scenes.say: Rubisco is a slow, clumsy worker. It sometimes grabs oxygen by mistake, causing photorespiration. Edits could make Rubisco faster, make Rubisco activase cope with heat, or cut photorespiration losses. Fewer stomata means less water lost. But less carbon dioxide gets in too, so mention the trade-off.
scenes.caption: Rubisco is a slow, clumsy worker. It sometimes grabs O₂ by mistake, causing photorespiration. Edits could make Rubisco faster, make Rubisco activase cope with heat, or cut photorespiration losses. Fewer stomata means less water lost. But less CO₂ gets in too, so always mention the trade-off.

scenes.heading: Bioethanol by fermentation
scenes.say: For biofuel: break, brew, boil. Cellulases break cellulose into glucose. Yeast brews it anaerobically into ethanol and carbon dioxide. Then the ethanol is distilled off. Keep oxygen out, or no ethanol is made.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: Edited yeast strain B tolerates ethanol and makes more ethanol than unedited strain A. Explain.
lines: High ethanol is toxic to yeast
Strain A stops at a toxic level
Ethanol toxicity, not glucose, was limiting
scenes.say: Both strains ferment glucose into ethanol. But ethanol is toxic to yeast at high levels, so strain A stops, even with glucose left. Strain B survives higher ethanol, so it keeps going. Ethanol toxicity, not glucose, was the limiting factor.

scenes.heading: Weighing it up

right.title: Limitations
points: Yield is controlled by many genes

scenes.say: For evaluate questions, give a benefit, a scientific limitation and an ethical point. CRISPR is precise and faster than traditional breeding. But watch for off-target effects, traits controlled by many genes, trade-offs, and questions like who owns edited seeds.

points: Guide RNA finds, Cas9 cuts, the cell fixes
Edit Rubisco or stomata for photosynthesis
scenes.say: Quick recap. Guide RNA finds, Cas9 cuts, the cell fixes. Edits to Rubisco or stomata could boost crops. Bioethanol comes from fermenting glucose. And always weigh up the limitations. Now try the practice questions!
